No. It looks like it would, doesn't it? Like it- No, but it's, well, it does absorb some water, but it filters out.

So it's hydrophobic. When you line it with plaster as well, then you've got a seal, haven't you? But it's sealed. Right. It'll meet the building code for weather-tight and water-tight and that sort of thing. Should I pass this down? Please. I feel like it, the microphones will pick up very distant.

There you go. Thanks, Margaret. They're not edibles. Morning, Richard. Really nice to see you back. What we were really after is an update on, since we've had you in last, how things have changed or not changed, and- Yes... what we may be able to do to assist the industry.

We've certainly seen some changes that the Ministry of Regulation announced actually not long after you presented to us last time. And there was some work going on between NPI and the Ministry of Health to make sure that some of the barriers that you raised were not going to be a barrier in the future. So, I'll leave it with you.

Well, I'm sure we're going to have an interesting conversation. Yeah. So thank you for the opportunity. I've just prepared to go along with the documents that we shared, just a brief statement so I can cover all the points. It'll only take about five or six minutes to read. So I'll just whip through that first- Okay... and then we can have some questions and I'll provide the answers. So Chair, members of the committee, thank you for the opportunity to appear before you today.

I'm speaking on behalf of the New Zealand Hemp Industries Association. Firstly, I'd like to acknowledge the committee's continued interest in industrial hemp. We appreciate your engagement over the past two years and the opportunity to continue the discussions following the recent regulatory reform. The association also appreciates the work undertaken by the Ministry of Regulation.

The review represented the first significant reform of industrial hemp regulations in 20 years. We publicly, excuse me, we publicly welcome those changes. Today, I'd like to briefly discuss three things, what has been achieved, what opportunities remain, and where government and industry can work together over the next two years.

Industrial hemp is no longer a simple agricultural crop. Around the world, it is becoming an important raw material for food, fiber, construction materials, as you can see with the hemp block, and internet, and textiles, bio composites, and the emerging bioeconomy. New Zealand has genuine competitive advantages. We already have world-class farming systems, excellent traceability, a strong research sector, and an international reputation for producing high-quality natural products.

The international market is growing rapidly. Our opportunity is not simply to grow, it is to build high-value processing industries and export both products and the technologies developed here in New Zealand. This is where the long-term economic value lies. The recent reforms removed one of the industry's biggest frustrations.

Replacing the Ministry of Health license with a notification process has significantly reduced compliant costs for growers and those processing seed. That was a practical and sensible decision, and increasing the THC to 1% has given us access to more genetics. Removing licenses has also attracted considerable international attention because New Zealand has demonstrated that industrial hemp can be regulated using a proportionate risk-based approach. For that, the industry is genuinely grateful.

However, these reforms primarily benefit cultivation, the growers, and the seed processors. They did not substantially improve opportunities for full plant utilization or manufacturing innovative products. The largest barrier today sits further along the value chain. Industrial hemp remains regulated under the Misuse of Drugs Act.

Oh. Despite the United Nations Single Convention specifically excluding low-THC industrial hemp grown for industrial and horticultural purposes. While growers can now produce the crop more easily, much of the plant cannot be used commercially except through the situation medicinal cannabis pathways.

That means that leaves and flowers and roots remain unavailable for health and wellness products. The current prohibition on hemp ingredients for production in companion animals also limits commercial opportunities and reduces full plant utilization. These restrictions make investment more difficult.

Businesses are reluctant to invest in processing infrastructure where large portions of the crop have no commercial pathway. CBD is now the central issue. From an industry perspective, THC is no longer the primary regulatory challenge, although getting out of MODA remains the NZHIA's number one objective.

Modern industrial hemp contains extremely low levels of THC and routinely tests well below regulatory thresholds. The remaining challenge is CBD. Because naturally occurring CBD is regulated as a prescription medicine under the Medicines Act, industrial hemp biomass can generally only enter the medicinal cannabis supply pathway.

Otherwise, we are forced to treat it as contaminant in our industrial hemp crops. This effectively prevents development of a broader health and wellness industry based on industrial hemp. Addressing this issue would unlock significant innovation while maintaining appropriate safeguards around therapeutic products. Growing hemp is only the first step.

The real economic opportunity lies in processing, manufacturing, and developing new products. That requires investment, it requires infrastructure, it requires research, and it requires confidence that regulations will continue evolving in a practical and evidence-based manner. The association is encouraged by the strong relationships we have developed with research organizations, universities, and innovation centers across New Zealand.

The capability exists. What is needed now is a regulatory environment that allows investment to follow. Looking ahead, the Ministry for Regulation has committed to reviewing these regulations again in two years. That provides an excellent opportunity. Between now and then, we can gather evidence, support responsible industry growth, and identify when further improvements can safely be made.

The NZHA is already contributing through education, industry guidance, and the New Zealand Hemp Industries Association Seed Product, helping new growers adopt best practices while maintaining industry integrity. Our requests, we respectfully ask the committee to continue supporting practical and evidence-based reform.

In particular, we encourage government to continue progressing, getting industrial hemp out of the Misuse of Drugs Act, finally allowing us to realize the full plant utilization and releasing us from the burdens and regulations. Review the treatment of naturally occurring CBD and low-THC industrial hemp that's leading to that health and wellness industry. Support development of a health products framework.

Revisit the restrictions of hemp for companion and production animals using evidence-based risk assessment. Support research, standards, and processing capability that will allow New Zealand to compete internationally and encourage investment into commercially viable hemp businesses and regional processing infrastructure.

These are practical steps that will help industry grow responsibly while creating regional jobs, supporting innovation, and contributing to New Zealand's emerging bio-economy. The 2026 reforms were an important milestone, and the industry sincerely thanks the government and officials for the progress that has been made, but they are only the beginning. We now have an opportunity to build a modern industrial hemp industry that delivers economic, environmental, and regional development benefits for New Zealand.

Our association looks forward to continuing to work constructively with government and with this committee ahead of the next review. Thank you, and over to questions. Thanks, Richard. We'll go straight to Mark Cameron, News. Good morning, Richard, and thank you so much for your time. We're very grateful for your time. I'm interested to know, obviously you'll have a pipeline of opportunity costs and opportunities gained.

Where do you see yourself in five years' time? We've certainly seen this committee very, very active in trying to create an environment that would give the hemp industry all the opportunities it deserves. But you surely to goodness have a pipeline of aspiration, and what does that look like? Well, if we're looking for a five-year horizon, then one of the milestones will be the review of the Ministry for Regulation's- Yeah changes that they made this year. So that's in two years' time.

So we'll be working towards that to provide the information and evidence to support the removal of low-THC industrial hemp out of the Misuse of Drugs Act, because we're just another agricultural, arable, or horticultural crop. Mm. And that would really free us up. So the regulations as they stand did make a difference for the grower.

They no longer need a license. They can just notify the police and Ministry of Primary Industries. So that's the supply chain. But that's not really where the bottleneck sits. It's the value chain is where we need to be developing innovative products. So in five years' time, I'd like to see pet foods available. Well, within one or two years, I would like to see pet foods available.

I'd like to see some trials done in the very short term on production animals, because we only have a very small amount of these co-products coming out of the hemp seed industry that could be used rather than being put into a 40-foot container and shipped overseas- Mm... or disposed in a landfill. So, full plant utilization means that we need the economics of all those parts of the plant to work in our favor, and we need access to those markets.

So working through with MPI, ACVM on the issue of production animals, which was ruled out of scope from the Ministry of Regulation's deliberations, so they couldn't do anything with that particular issue. Now, that was one of the biggest issues facing the industry. So great, the growers are moving forward, but without those markets, it's very burdensome still in the sense that we don't have access to the economics that we need. So the animal food issue would be a great one to overcome in the next five years.

And this treatment of CBD as a prescription medicine under the Medicines Act complicates things unnecessary for industrial hemp. The medicinal cannabis scheme has its own way of doing things. They have their own regulatory involvement with the Ministry of Health. We are now no longer really involved with the Ministry of Health unless we want to import or export because of that low level of THC.

But going back to the CBD, it's a massive problem because it's naturally occurring in our plant, as are a number of other cannabinoids that all have commercial interest, along with terpenes and flavonoids. So not being able to make products from the leaf and the flower and the roots is a massive problem.

So our arable industry for food and fiber, that's going to continue to go ahead, as we've discussed, without the need for a license. That's removed again, a burdensome regulation that cost money for compliance. So that's gone. But when we look at the horticultural industry, which is this part where we're looking at these health and wellness products, it's really problematic because there's global demand for them. There's Demand in New Zealand for them.

But we can't access that market because of the treatment of the Medicines Act making CBD a prescription medicine. Now, at certain high doses, it probably is a therapeutic and a medicine. But when it's naturally occurring in the plant, we can't take it out, but it's restricting us. So, there's a room, in the association's opinion, for the Ministry of Health to look at the Medicines Act and look at the Medicinal Cannabis scheme and say, "Except for industrial hemp," something like that.

But again, removing us as a prohibitive plant from the Misuse of Drugs Act would also aid that as well, because we're not a drug, we're an arable and cultural crop. So in five years' time, you could open up sort of all sorts of opportunities, and significant money would be involved because you're leading to export-led market development. And that's where our aspirational goals and the things like Dr. Nick Marsh's investment strategies in 2020. When the Ministry for regulation came in and spoke to you, it was like, "Oh, the industry's worth about a

million." Well, industry thinks it's worth about 9 or 10 million currently, but that could really expand in the near future if we had access to these markets. The markets that will continue to grow, given our current regulatory settings, would be in the fiber and the food side. But with this document in 2020, the biggest number in there for export potential was in that health and wellness products, because these are small items, highly valuable, making use of our provenance story, enhancing New Zealand with quality export products

backed by the New Zealand farming systems, which are world-class, and introducing traceability and those sort of things in there. So those would be the things in five years' time I would like to see those markets open up. And with regard to the fiber, it would be great to see the hempcrete block and hempcrete building materials and other building materials, the insulation materials, all coming from those parts of the fiber of the stem of the plant. And from a food point of view, gaining more traction, getting them recognized in the mainstream, working on

economies of scale. So this is where the opportunity to work with genetics, one way to increase a farmer's return is increase the yield that they could get. So a bit of the breeding going on there for the seed yield and things like that. But also looking at what makes New Zealand hemp special. Given our growing environment, given our light and our volcanic soils and things, is there ways that we can differentiate ourselves in the market globally? I see the hemp seed oil particularly as that's a global commodity, and that could get up there with the wine

industry, where we work together and keep the standards high for consumers overseas and overseas markets. And these overseas markets are developing. This industry is one of probably the few industries currently that are growing at double-digit compound annual growth rates. So that's been the story for the last 10 to 15 years.

So if that continues, which it will, then there's real economic opportunities out there for us. So in five years' time, I'd like to see it, yeah, getting close to the aspirations of moving it way beyond the $30 million mentioned in another report, and growing from there. Thank you, Richard. Brilliant. Barbara, you had a question.

Yeah. It's kind of frustrating because that piece in the middle is missing. One of the things that over the years, the Natural Health Products Bill has dragged on and on and on to the point where, say a few months ago, could have been longer, it was actually withdrawn in terms of being able to make it useful again.

And so it seems to be from a health perspective, they talk about a billion-dollar industry that's got caught up with New Zealand regulations that sits under Health. What association have you had with any other industries around the natural health products? I think there seems to be an opportunity here to work together to get that part of it right, because it seems silly to me that we can grow it- And not use it... we can't make something out of it.

And I know there's lots of other people in that natural health product space that have that same issue. So are you connected with them in any way? Yes, we work with the Natural Health Products Association. Yeah. And they're following it with interest. And we're happy to, again, like hemp is part of the bioeconomy from a fiber point of view and a food point of view, same with the natural health products.

We're just one of a number of natural health products which would benefit from having a natural health products framework. Mm. And if we can achieve that, then the rising tide lifts all boats. So, yes, we would definitely be calling for it, and we'll be supporting their endeavors as much as we can, and putting forward the economic case of adding hemp to existing natural health products.

There's a massive industry already exists, and it's a very collegial industry in the sense that they're making products that are similar or competitive, but they're all doing it together. And it's a bit of a New Zealand way of doing it because you can go, we could tap into NZTE, you could go overseas with it, you join others.

And really, you're obviously promoting your product, but by promoting the sector, it all grows. And there's some things we can do under the Dietary Supplements Act as well. But again, it comes back to this treatment of CBD because if that's detected, then it's a problem. Yeah. The reason for asking that question, Mr. Chair, is there's a roadblock there in the health, I think the health, some conversation, this group and the health committee might be useful, because farm- That was going to be my next question, actually, yeah

... yeah, the growers are losing a lot. So, how much interaction you had with the Ministry of Health to- Resolve this, and how supportive do you think they are of getting this roadblock cleared? I think we've had quite a lot of interactions with the Ministry of Health, of course, about the Industrial Hemp Regulations 2006 that ultimately were reformed into 2026.

Mm-hmm. That's probably taken up lots of the energy for it. The Ministry of Health were in favor of, as we were, of removing hemp from needing a license, which was option four from the Ministry for regulation, which was a bold move. They no longer require a license. That's international news.

The thing about that is that they've been quite successful because they don't want to deal with an arable crop or a horticultural crop. Mm. And our farmers don't want to deal with the Ministry of Health amongst everybody else that they have to deal with. So there's a win there. But the conversation gets bogged down with our connection as cannabis to the Misuse of Drugs Act, THC, as we've described. We're semi out of that because they realize it's low risk. They're not interested in an arable crop.

So if we look for the horticultural crop, back to your question, Barbara, about the natural health products, then it becomes problematic because of the way they've treated CBD and the Medicines Act. So now we're being knocked on the head with that. So that's why I say it's one of the major issues facing us. So with regard to dialogue with them, we're working on some approaches, and it's just the people that we've been dealing with in the Medsafe, and the medicinal cannabis, and industrial hemp sort of area that looks after the administration, there's not a lot they can

do because they're looking at a piece of legisl- you know, the regulations and going, "Well, we can only do what we can do in that." So it becomes a policy issue, which comes down to political will. So when we started this process in 2023 with the strategic document, and I did a whole lot of meetings in '24, came to the Primary Production Select Committee then.

It has cross-party support. Yes, there's still some stigma around it because some people just hear hemp and jump straight to cannabis, straight to marijuana, and it's a problem. But the people that are aware of the construction materials and all these other materials, and again, if we're focusing on the natural health products, there's growing market demand for those products.

So it's quite frustrating for the industry not to be able to access them. To get access to them would require political will. So you don't see that sector having a lot of opposition from the medical experts, et cetera, if at some stage we decide to change the leg or the regulations around the horticulture uses. You don't think there will be an outcry from them?

From the Ministry of Health point of view, again, the reluctance around a natural health products framework would exist for our products as well. But that said, though, at the high doses that an isolate put into a medicine, and it's a CBD or a THC medicine-... that's right up there. But generally, we can quote the UN as- Yeah... Single Convention is not interested in CBD at all.

WHO and the European community have said that CBD is non-addictive, it's a safe product. So at naturally occurring levels in a plant, then there shouldn't be too much pushback. And we're not making medical claims, so we're not wanting to be part of the therapeutic framework. We just want to have access to the health and wellness products. And CBD is stopping the consumer getting involved with not only limited amounts of CBD and hemp, but it's all these minor cannabinoids, these terpenes and flavonoids, that also have constructive commercial uses, but

make wonderful products that are of use to people in that market of that health and wellness market. Thank you. Rachel. So there'll be some issues, but we can overcome that. Yeah. Yeah. And we touched on it a little bit, but I'm just interested in knowing if you do regular research into public views, because I think that you touched on it before about how people hear hemp and often think something quite different. And so I'm just wondering on that public, have you been tracking the kind of understanding and views of the public

over the last few years in terms of how they see hemp? We're a voluntary organization, so we- So you don't have the resources to do that. That would be one observation. But over the years, you can see it. For a period there, people wouldn't say to me, "Can I smoke my hat?" When I was selling hats at the market and things like that. Yeah. But that's a reaction similar to what with the Brit.

It's a reaction people have. Yes. But it reinforces that stigma and- Yeah... this is where the work from the Ministry for Regulation really did help as well because it gave the credibility to industrial hemp. And we're not going to turn around and start calling it hemp as the regulation suggests now, because it's always industrial hemp, and that perception- Yeah... is important for the consumer to understand.

Yeah. And the reluctance of some people for the food industry, "Am I going to fail a drug test if I eat hemp seed oil?" No, you're not. But it was a question. So, we needed more education there, and that's something that the Ministry of Health's announcement helped with. But there's other ways that we could do that as well.

It could be in the government procurement. If you want healthy school lunches, maybe start using hemp seed in your lunches. If you want green and healthy and sustainable buildings, start thinking about hempcrete. Help us with those standards to get that information out there. So there's some really good things we can do. But the cons- If I looked at it from a 20-year or 30-year perspective, it's massively different now. People aren't as full of reefer madness and anti-marijuana crossing over to hemp as they are. They can see the difference.

We're not marijuana. We're very low THC, and so that is helping, and it's gaining traction. When I talk to hemp now, it's about, oh, hempcrete, or it's about protruded fiber products and rebar that they're making out of it for construction. All these sustainable uses in these heavily intensive CO2 sort of situations. Those industries that aren't that sustainable when using fossil fuels, whereas the consumer, I think, is coming around to realizing that they can grow annually- Mm... what we need- Mm... rather than extracting it as a fossil fuel.

Mm. And Henry Ford said, "Whatever you can make out of hydrocarbons, you can make out of carbohydrates." So if they could do that in the 19th century, or the 20th century rather, I'm sure we can do very well now. So it's an opportunity, and that's where New Zealand lies. Our R&D ecosystem is absolutely engaged. They just need to have, obviously, industry support, but government support towards doing some foundational work would lead to all sorts of commercial opportunities, and especially in the fiber- Yes... into construction materials, composites, plastics.

These lightweight things are really gaining traction. Graphene, replacing graphene in batteries, that sort of thing. You can make it all out of hemp, and we've got a really good understanding, and that ecosystem, as I say, from New Zealand Product Accelerator, the bioscience, the new CRIs all coming together, they're all very engaged with it.

And so they're wanting to use that significant resource of 1,700 odd scientists to really apply it, and that's New Zealand's gift to the world because if we did embrace it, we could be using it to make the processing equipment, the tech, and then you license that overseas because everybody in the world is trying to scale their industry. And we're successfully doing so.

The Carfields have brought on a decorticator. There's another two decorticators, one at Hemp Central in Wanaka, and Venture Taranaki. So that's now stimulating the fiber side. But to scale into the realms of competing with fossil fuels as a raw material for industry, you've got to scale up, and this is a real opportunity for us. And all that equipment needs to be developed and understood.

We're still using 20th century technology, early 20th century technology. Sue. Fantastic submission. Thank you very much, and really appreciate your passion for the industry. Thank you. So, simply put, the first task is to get it out of the Misuse of Drugs Act. Is that right? Would that- That's our number one objective... make a significant difference in terms of your return on investment and your, and everything that you- Future growth, yeah... and future growth and cost of production.

I imagine it's impeding your cost of production too, the regulatory frameworks, maybe? Well, in the sense that it's halting a whole sector. Yeah. Holding the growth. And then I was interested in that you were, in your submission, in fact, it could be said we're now further away than when the definitions of industrial hemp and hemp products were in place under the 2006 regulations. So it's got worse before it's got better.

In a sense, yes, because under the 2006 industrial regulations, the hemp definition of a hemp product was anything made from hemp, and hemp was-- Sorry, industrial hemp it was called then, which is low THC industrial hemp. Yeah. So we could make any product. So I could make a case for making a natural health product. Then I would have to deal with the end use legislation the same as I would with food or the building code for fiber and things. Whereas now they've changed, the Ministry of Health have taken an opportunity to tighten that definition.

So hemp product is now can't be made from all parts of the plant. It's only the stem and the seed. So then you're left with the leaf and the roots, and the flower of the plant, which previously I could've made a case for being able to be used in a market. Now we have a new baseline on our not so level playing field that says, "No, you can't."

You must supply that to a medicinal cannabis company. Or presumably, we may be able to export it, and bypass the New Zealand economy to the straight away, go global from day one. So which is great for the global community, but not so good for New Zealand. So that's why I referred to that. It has made it a little bit more difficult.

But it has given us that new baseline, so we know where we stand. Roots was always a bit, in the gray area. We argued that the roots are part of the stem, so they're a stem, and the stems were always a hemp product and there was no restrictions. But now they've taken the opportunity to tell us, "No, that's your new..." So we've got this baseline. This is where we're working for.

We know where we stand now in 2026. What can we do? What can we prove? Evidence we can raise, arguments that we can put together, to justify changing it within that two-year review. So that two-year review is very, very important for the industry because that brings into light an opportunity to have this conversation again somewhere, and show where the world's gone, where these products could've been, because that's the opportunity cost we're missing.

Right. Final questions, Steve. Mine's sort of a bit of an observation, whether you want to respond or not, but I feel like the paradox of hemp and cannabis more broadly is that its problem is it does too many things. It's such a super species that you can make clothes from it- Oh, well- ...

you can make building materials from it, you can eat it, it's medicinal, it does all the things, and that's actually part of its challenge. And so it seems that we have to get over the, we have to-- It's kind of ridiculous that we find ourselves in a situation where we can't utilize it because it does everything. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Which is very frustrating. And the hemp industry, what is the hemp industry? Well, it's part of the food industry, it's part of the building industry, it's part of the composite industry, health and wellness industry, as we discussed.

So yeah, we've got too many points, not enough penetration. But that's a-- The industry will drive that, the people passionate in those areas about food or about composite materials or about graphene or plastics, textiles. They'll push it for themselves. Mm. Mm. So, that's where the investment from our point of view, particularly in fiber, comes in because that's the primary processing step.

We need that infrastructure to get out the two commodities that then can feed into those, some of those channels, as can seed. But in seed's case, we can't use animals, so changing the companion animals, production animal situation is probably equally as important for many members as the CBD situation. So that's the one that we can really work on with you guys at the Primary Production Select Committee, because having a ban on both production and companion doesn't make sense because of the perceived trade risk.

That only involves production, so free up companion. Perceived trade risk. Is there any evidence for that? No. Have they done any work to quantify the problem? These are really big issues. So those two issues are the big ones- Okay, right... CBD and animal foods. Don't leave the pets and dogs. Thanks very much, Richard. I really appreciate you, as Sue said, your passion and your advocacy for the industry.

Thank you. That was really useful to get that briefing, give us an understanding of where we're at and where we need to go. So thank you very much. Thank you for the opportunity, sir. I had the final briefing picked right up on those two points because we'll carry on working on them, but with your support-... political will- Yeah... we can get there. No. Thank you so much. Thank you, guys. It'd be good to untie one of your hands from behind your back so you can go for it.
Exactly. I wonder if that, if that, I was trying to think if the, not the Hasno, the other one with health-
